subject: english-language
title: Modal Verbs and FANBOYS
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on modal verbs and coordinating conjunctions.
final_note: You can now use modal verbs and remember FANBOYS.

concepts.def: Joins equal parts of a sentence.
For And Nor But Or Yet So.
Two simple sentences joined by FANBOYS.

walkthroughs.body_html: Modals: can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would. They show ability ('can swim') or obligation ('must run').
FANBOYS = For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. These coordinating conjunctions join equal clauses to make compound sentences.
'I wanted cake, but the shop was shut.' Two equal clauses joined with a FANBOY = a compound sentence.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between voiced and voiceless sounds?
options: The cooperative principle means everyone must agree in conversation.
Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.
Voiced sounds are loud and voiceless sounds are whispered.
Voiced sounds are produced with vocal-fold vibration (/b/, /d/, /g/, /z/); voiceless sounds without it (/p/, /t/, /k/, /s/). You can feel the difference by putting a hand on your throat.
The cooperative principle means everyone must agree in conversation.
Standard English is the same as Received Pronunciation.
The cooperative principle means people are always nice to each other.
The assumption that speakers cooperate in conversation by following maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner — flouting these creates implicature.
Standard English is the original and correct form of the language.
